qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture three. Storage and retrieval. This is how a database keeps data on disk, and finds it again.
Some work is many small writes, such as orders.
Some work is many small writes.
Other work is one big read, scanning every row for one answer.
Other work is one big read.
The right design depends on the workload.
Design follows the workload.
A log is a file you only add to, one line at a time.
A log is a file you only add to.
A set adds a line at the end. The old bike line stays.
Set adds a line at the end.
A get scans the lines, and the last line for the key wins.
Get scans for the last line of a key.
A delete adds a tombstone line. Nothing is erased.
Delete adds a tombstone line.
The newest line for dock is the tombstone, so it says deleted.
The newest line says: deleted.
A write is one append, so one step.
A write is one append: one step.
A read scans every line, because the match could be the last.
A read scans every line.
Twice the data, twice the scan. That is big O of n.
Twice the data, twice the scan.
So a log needs an index to skip the scan.
We need an index.
Keep a map in memory, from each key to the byte offset where its line starts.
Keep a map in memory: key to byte offset.
To get mew, look up its offset.
Get mew: look up its offset.
Then jump straight there. One disk read, not nine.
One jump, one disk read.
A write appends a line, here for purr.
A write appends a line.
Then the map is updated, so purr points to the new line.
Every write updates the map.
So getting purr is still one jump.
Get purr: still one jump.
A log that only grows will fill the disk.
A log that only grows fills the disk.
So a file is closed at its size limit, and a new one opens.
So close a file at its size limit.
There are twelve records, but only three keys.
Many records, only three keys.
Compaction keeps the latest value of each key, so twelve records become three.
Compaction keeps the latest value per key.
The map must fit in memory, and only six of twelve keys do.
The whole map must fit in memory.
A range needs one lookup per key, because the map has no order.
A range needs one lookup per key.
Sorted keys sit side by side, so a range is one stretch.
Sorted keys sit side by side.
Three sorted segments, oldest on the left, each with every key once.
Three sorted segments, oldest left.
A ring marks the next key in each segment. The smallest is apple.
Take the smallest key first.
Apple is in two segments. The newest wins, so apple one is dropped.
Repeats: the newest wins.
For kiwi, the newest copy is a tombstone, so kiwi is written nowhere.
A newer tombstone deletes it.
Repeat for fig, mango and plum, until every segment is used up.
Repeat until every segment is used up.
Ten records went in. Four come out, sorted, with no old values.
One sorted segment, no old values.
This segment is sorted by key, in three blocks of four.
A segment sorted by key.
So the index keeps just the first key of each block, three of twelve.
The index holds only some keys.
To find handbag, jump to the nearest indexed key before it, hand.
Jump to the key before it.
Then scan a short block. Two reads find handbag.
Scan a short block.
For a range, jump once, then read on until a key is past the end.
A range: one jump, read on.
Writes arrive in any order, and land in memory first.
Writes land in memory first.
A memtable is a tree. Smaller keys go left, bigger go right.
A tree keeps the keys in order.
When it is full, it is written to disk in order.
When full, write it out in order.
New writes go to a fresh memtable.
New writes get a new memtable.
A read checks memory first, then the newest segment.
Reads check memory, then newest.
The first hit wins. Fig is eleven, and the old eight is never read.
First hit wins: fig 11, not 8.
A log writes fast, but a read has to scan every line.
An index in memory jumps straight to the data.
Sorted segments merge easily, and need only a sparse index.
